Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) is among the most lethal solid tumors [@siegel2026cancer], and its clinical heterogeneity reflects variation in both malignant cells and the surrounding microenvironment. Bulk transcriptomic studies have identified clinically relevant malignant and stromal states in PDAC, including basal-like and classical tumor programs [@collisson2011subtypes; @moffitt2015virtual; @rashid2020purity] and, from single-cell-informed analyses, tumor-promoting proCAF and tumor-restraining restCAF stromal programs [@peng2024determination]. Single-cell and spatial profiling have further shown that this heterogeneity extends across malignant, stromal, immune, and other microenvironmental compartments within individual tumors [@moncada2020spatial; @hwang2022single; @werba2023single]. Most transcriptomic programs in PDAC have been defined from expression patterns and only subsequently related to outcome [@collisson2011subtypes; @Bailey2016]. It remains unclear whether using survival information during discovery can characterize programs that add prognostic information beyond established classifications. Such programs could support prognostic assay development and trial stratification, while highlighting genes and biological processes for downstream validation and clinical application.

Addressing this question often requires large cohorts with survival-annotated transcriptomic data, which in PDAC are still derived primarily from bulk profiling [@aung2018compass]. Bulk profiles, however, mix signals from malignant and microenvironmental cells [@nguyen2024fourteen]. Nonnegative matrix factorization (NMF) and related deconvolution methods represent these composite profiles as combinations of gene programs, defined by weighted sets of co-varying genes that together form a representation of the tumor transcriptome, alongside sample-specific program usage indicating how strongly each program contributes to each tumor. In PDAC, these approaches have supported molecular subtype discovery and subsequent single-sample classification [@collisson2011subtypes; @Bailey2016; @rashid2020purity], virtual microdissection of tumor- and stroma-specific expression [@moffitt2015virtual], and compartment-specific tumor--stroma characterization [@peng2019novo; @peng2024determination]. Incorporating survival into program discovery could instead resolve prognostic signal into distinct gene programs, helping identify the biological processes associated with outcome and whether those same programs recur across independent cohorts.

Standard NMF learns gene-program weights and sample-specific program usage by minimizing reconstruction error, the mismatch between the measured expression matrix and the expression reconstructed from the product of those program weights and usages. Such reconstruction-driven criteria favor patterns that capture prominent expression variation regardless of their relevance to patient survival [@bair2004semi; @cook2007fisher]. This is particularly important in PDAC, where bulk tumors contain substantial stromal, exocrine, and other non-malignant signals that can dominate transcriptomic variation and obscure less prominent but prognostically relevant programs [@rashid2020purity; @torrehealy2023pdacr; @peng2024determination; @aran2015systematic].

Because NMF decompositions are not unique, different solutions can reconstruct the same expression data comparably well while defining the underlying gene programs differently [@donoho2004nmf; @laurberg2008uniqueness; @gillis2014nmf]. This ambiguity may contribute to the variation among proposed unsupervised PDAC subtype taxonomies [@lautizi2022pancreatic]. The basal-like/classical dichotomy itself emerged through roughly a decade of iterative subtyping, virtual microdissection, independent cohorts, single-cell analyses and prospective clinical profiling [@collisson2011subtypes; @moffitt2015virtual; @rashid2020purity; @werba2023single; @aung2018compass], and comparable refinement of stromal CAF subtypes is ongoing [@peng2024determination]. Existing survival-supervised models such as penalized Cox regression and supervised principal components generally identify outcome-associated genes or linear combinations of genes rather than decomposing expression into interpretable gene programs [@bair2004semi; @simon2011regularization]. This distinction is particularly relevant in PDAC, where malignant and stromal gene programs underlie established molecular subtypes [@rashid2020purity; @peng2024determination].

Here, we present DeSurv, a survival-supervised matrix factorization framework that integrates NMF with Cox regression, allowing survival information to influence gene-program discovery while retaining a decomposed representation of the transcriptome. Because the factorization is sensitive to initialization, solutions from many independent restarts are aggregated to initialize a final fit. The resulting gene weights are then held fixed, or frozen, so that the same learned programs can be evaluated in external cohorts without refitting the representation.

We evaluate DeSurv in PDAC by comparing the resulting representation with unsupervised NMF at matched and higher rank, where rank is the number of programs the factorization extracts, and with conventional supervised survival models such as penalized Cox regression and supervised principal components (Supplementary Table \ref{tab:architecture}). We then evaluate the clinical relevance of the learned programs in independent cohorts and ask whether they retain prognostic information beyond established PDAC classifiers. Simulations in which the true underlying (latent) programs are known characterize the conditions under which incorporating survival into factorization improves recovery of prognostic structure.
